Header:
Date: 2026-04-22
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luca Moretti (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Alder - Head of ML), Tom Alvarez (Alder - Platform), Sophie Kim (Alder - CTO)

Optional auto sections present: Summary, Action items, Next steps (recorded separately)

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros - I'm Maya, AE on the account, and Luca is our SE who will run the technical demo.
[00:00:12] Priya Singh: Hi, Priya here, thanks for squeezing us in. We're real curious about the long context stuff and also, we have pretty spiky traffic.
[00:00:20] Luca Moretti: Great, we'll focus on both. Agenda: 1) long context / KV caching behavior, 2) high TPS and batching, 3) streaming backpressure and client-side timeouts, 4) fallback strategies.
[00:00:35] Tom Alvarez: Quick note: our SLO is 95th latency under 200ms for short generation, and for the long context flows we can tolerate up to 500-700ms but with correct state.
[00:00:45] Maya Chen: Got it. Also, budget constraints flagged by Sophie - they're sensitive to per-token cost spikes during bursts.
[00:00:55] Sophie Kim: Yes that's right, we want predictable unit economics.
[00:01:10] Luca Moretti: Okay jumping into the demo - I'm sharing the Console. First, long context. We support pinned KV cache and prefix caching; for very long contexts we recommend chunked retrieval and streaming so you don't re-send the entire 100k token history each request.
[00:01:30] Priya Singh: Wait, 100k tokens? we were planning to store conversation history up to around 60k tokens, but some of our batch jobs append long doc contexts so, yea - how does that look in practice?
[00:01:40] Luca Moretti: In practice we do two things: 1) continuous KV cache so the model's past attention keys are kept on the GPU between requests, that avoids re-embedding the whole context; 2) for document-level context we recommend retrieval-augmented generation where you pass only the retrieved chunks plus a short in-memory prefix.
[00:01:55] Maya Chen: (note: transcription sometimes shows "K V cash" in auto captions) apologies for the auto-caption artifacts.
[00:02:08] Tom Alvarez: Can you explain memory/per-GPU constraints? If we have very long KV caches per session, how many concurrent sessions can each GPU support?
[00:02:18] Luca Moretti: Good question. It depends on model and quantization. With 8-bit quant and our runtime optimizations, we see X sessions for a 70B class model - in your case for heavier contexts we recommend pinned tokens per session capped, and offload cold KV pages to SSD to avoid OOM; there's a tradeoff for latency when a cache miss happens.
[00:02:40] Priya Singh: When you say "offload to SSD" - is that automatic? what's the latency penalty?
[00:02:48] Luca Moretti: It's configurable. Typical cold page fetch adds 30-100ms depending on storage and network. We instrument per-key fetch timings in the Console and surface them in the tracing dashboard.
[00:02:58] Sophie Kim: That 30-100ms could blow our p95. How do you recommend we handle that from an app perspective?
[00:03:10] Luca Moretti: We recommend a few patterns: async warm-up when you detect a session coming back online, or keeping a small hot set of recent contexts in memory and moving the rest to cold store. Also fallback model variants for degraded latency - e.g., route to a smaller 7B variant if the large model is blocked.
[00:03:30] Maya Chen: Let's pivot to high TPS. Priya mentioned spiky traffic - what's the peak TPS you're expecting?
[00:03:38] Priya Singh: We plan for steady 200 rps for embeddings and bursts to 1k rps for chat generation during business hours, with sustained bursts of up to ~2 minutes.
[00:03:48] Tom Alvarez: Also want to run a smoke test at 2k sustained for 10m during onboarding to validate autoscaling and fallback.
[00:03:56] Luca Moretti: Understood. Our Dedicated pools provide predictable throughput - autoscaling policies can spin additional nodes within configured burst capacity. For API mode we enforce per-customer concurrency controls; you can set per-route TPS caps and burst windows.
[00:04:12] Priya Singh: How does batching interact with latency targets? we can't batch too long or p95 jumps.
[00:04:20] Luca Moretti: We use latency-aware dynamic batching. If the queue builds up for a few ms, the runtime will batch to increase throughput but it respects per-request latency deadlines. You can configure max batch delay (e.g., 5-20ms). For your 200ms p95 target we usually recommend max batch delay under 10ms for generation.
[00:04:40] Sophie Kim: Are there cases where batching causes token interleaving or context mixing?
[00:04:46] Luca Moretti: No token mixing; each request keeps its own KV and attention. Batching only merges compute for efficiency. We've seen mis-perceptions in transcripts where people hear "token mixing" - it's not happening.
[00:04:58] Maya Chen: Now streaming behavior and backpressure - Luca will demo a simulated client that pauses read after a few chunks.
[00:05:08] Luca Moretti: I'm switching to the streaming test harness. We're using chunked SSE over HTTP/2 in this demo - clients can pause processing which creates backpressure. Redwood's runtime supports per-connection send buffers with configurable high/low watermarks. If a connection crosses high watermark we start adaptive throttling and can trigger backpressure signals upstream.
[00:05:28] Tom Alvarez: Does that mean the request blocks on the GPU and reduces overall concurrency?
[00:05:35] Luca Moretti: Potentially yes, if streaming is synchronous and client isn't reading, the server will hold the output tokens. To mitigate we offer configurable strategies: 1) drop streaming (fail fast) after a timeout, 2) switch to non-streaming buffered response where we buffer up to N tokens and close early, 3) spool to a persistent message queue and return a job id.
[00:05:55] Priya Singh: We're concerned about head-of-line blocking during big bursts if many clients are paused.
[00:06:02] Luca Moretti: For that we recommend per-connection quotas and an admission control layer that prefers short-running requests. There's also a circuit-breaker to evict low-priority streams when pressure is high.
[00:06:15] Priya Singh: In the demo I saw the label "max_stream_duration" - is that configurable per route?
[00:06:21] Luca Moretti: Yes, per route and per-customer. Default in our demo is 30s, but you can set it lower. For long documents we recommend chunked RPC where you request the next chunk explicitly.
[00:06:33] Sophie Kim: What about client-side timeouts and retries - best practice?
[00:06:38] Luca Moretti: Best practice: short client read timeouts for streaming chunks (e.g., 5-10s), exponential backoff on reconnect with jitter, and idempotency tokens for retriable requests. For generation requests that modify state, use a session/tokens pattern.
[00:06:52] Tom Alvarez: Do you support gRPC bidi streaming as well?
[00:06:56] Luca Moretti: Yes, we support gRPC as an alternative; gRPC allows more fine-grained flow control which helps with backpressure. Note some customers prefer SSE over gRPC due to firewall/proxy constraints.
[00:07:08] Priya Singh: Any noted differences in latency between gRPC and HTTP/1 streaming?
[00:07:12] Luca Moretti: gRPC/H2 tends to be more stable under high-concurrency because of flow control; HTTP/1 chunked is more fragile through proxies.
[00:07:22] Maya Chen: Quick interjection - security ask from Sophie: encryption, KMS, audit logs - Luca, can you summarize?
[00:07:30] Luca Moretti: Sure. For Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key management, TLS in transit, per-route RBAC, and immutable audit logs that we can forward to your SIEM. For Hosted we offer SOC2, VPC peering options, and customer-managed keys for Enterprise tiers. We'll share the security whitepaper.
[00:07:50] Sophie Kim: Good. Also want to understand data residency - we have EU-only requirements for a subset of workloads.
[00:07:56] Maya Chen: We have region pinning and private control plane options - can separate EU-only routes and dedicated nodes.
[00:08:05] Priya Singh: Back to the timeout story - what are fallback semantics when a generation times out? we can't return partial tokens that confuse our downstream scoring.
[00:08:13] Luca Moretti: We support three fallback semantics: 1) partial-chunk abort with a clear error code so clients know to discard partial tokens, 2) return last stable checkpoint and a null flag, 3) synchronous fallback model where if the primary times out we try a smaller variant and return that result if it completes within your overall deadline. We recommend clear contract in the client library to avoid inconsistent partial outputs.
[00:08:36] Tom Alvarez: Can we run a pilot where we exercise all three semantics and measure our app's behavior?
[00:08:42] Maya Chen: Absolutely - that's the plan. We'll run a 2-week pilot with a smoke test at 2k rps and guided tests for long-context KV cache correctness.
[00:08:55] Priya Singh: Great. A couple of clarifying Qs - for billing, how are buffered tokens billed during streaming when client pauses?
[00:09:03] Luca Moretti: We bill on tokens generated. If a token is generated and emitted, it's billable. If a stream is aborted before generation of some tokens, those tokens aren't billed. If you use spooling/async jobs we have different billing for queued vs served tokens; we'll show specifics in the pricing sheet.
[00:09:20] Sophie Kim: Any competitor limitations we should be aware of? we talked to Anthropic and they had strict session limits, OpenAI had rate-limiting that affected demo scale.
[00:09:28] Maya Chen: We'll include a comparison doc; in our experience Redwood gives more knobs for batching and KV retention which helps high- TPS predictable economics.
[00:09:40] Priya Singh: Can you demo a short streaming pause and show how the system behaves?
[00:09:45] Luca Moretti: Sure. Starting a sample stream now...
[00:09:58] [demo noise: harness logs, network graphs, occasional beep]
[00:10:05] Luca Moretti: Pausing client read now... you can see the connection buffer growing in the Console, green -> amber -> red threshold. At red threshold the runtime emits a backpressure metric and we start applying eviction of low-priority streams.
[00:10:20] Tom Alvarez: The graph shows per-GPU buffer fill - in our prod we need visibility into that metric.
[00:10:26] Luca Moretti: It's in Console under "runtime metrics" and you can set alerts/SLI on buffer_highwater_pct.
[00:10:35] Priya Singh: Can alerts trigger automated fallback to smaller models?
[00:10:39] Luca Moretti: Yes, via routing policy rules: if buffer_highwater_pct > X and latency > Y then route new requests to fallback model. You can put canary/weighting too.
[00:10:49] Sophie Kim: Sounds good. Any gotchas on retried requests causing duplicate effects?
[00:10:53] Luca Moretti: Use idempotency keys. For any stateful operation our SDK supports session tokens to avoid duplicates.
[00:11:02] Priya Singh: Ok role-based access - can we restrict who can change route policies?
[00:11:06] Maya Chen: Yes, RBAC in Console supports granular permissions - we'll include a screenshot in the security doc.
[00:11:15] Tom Alvarez: For the pilot we want to run the following: 1) 2-week pilot, 2) stress test 2k rps for 10m once, 3) run backpressure pause tests and measure client behavior, 4) validate KV cache correctness on 60-100k token sessions.
[00:11:30] Maya Chen: Sounds reasonable. We'll send a pilot proposal and pricing.
[00:11:36] Priya Singh: Timeline - we'd like to start the pilot next week. Is that feasible?
[00:11:40] Maya Chen: Yes, we can start with a sandbox Dedicated pool. Luca, any setup time?
[00:11:44] Luca Moretti: We can provision a sandbox in 48-72h once network connectivity and IP allowlist are set. For Private deployments it takes longer but for Dedicated sandbox it's quick.
[00:11:56] Sophie Kim: Please share the list of required IPs and SSO configs.
[00:12:00] Maya Chen: Will do.
[00:12:05] [side chatter - people typing, link shares]
[00:12:22] Maya Chen: Quick recap and next steps: 1) Redwood send pilot pricing + benchmark config (Maya) 2) Redwood send security whitepaper and network diagram (Maya/Luca) 3) SE to provide test harness and sample client for backpressure tests (Luca) 4) Alder to share prompt set and success criteria (Priya) 5) schedule pilot kickoff (all)
[00:12:45] Priya Singh: Yep, we'll send prompts by Friday.
[00:12:50] Tom Alvarez: Also add billing contact and trial limits to the kickoff invite.
[00:12:55] Maya Chen: Noted. Any final Qs?
[00:13:00] Sophie Kim: No, thanks - that was helpful.
[00:13:05] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the doc bundle and calendar invite.
[00:13:10] [meeting ends - remainder of the call was admin wrap up and scheduling]

Notes on transcription: occasional auto-caption errors ("K V cash" for KV cache, some proper nouns mis-typed). Transcript intentionally retains conversational fillers and small interruptions.
